lead: Every channel has a job. A few you must know by number: 16, 70, 13 and the intership channels. The rest you look up. And whichever channel you choose, VHF reaches only as far as your antenna can see.

sections.title: The channel you watch and call on

qa.q: Can I chat with another yacht on channel 16?
qa.a: No: **channel 16** is for distress, urgency, safety and calling. Call the yacht on 16, agree a working channel and both move there at once; only distress traffic stays on 16.

blocks.p: **Channel 16** is the international channel for distress, urgency, safety and calling. Under way you keep the radio on 16 even when you have nothing to say: that is how you hear a MAYDAY, a safety warning or someone calling you.

It is a meeting place, not a place to talk. You call a station on 16, agree a working channel and both move there at once. Only distress traffic stays on 16: a MAYDAY and the replies to it. While that goes on, keep off 16 altogether and make routine calls straight on the working channel: a marina's own channel, or the one your flotilla agreed beforehand.

blocks.rule: Call on 16, talk elsewhere. During a MAYDAY, keep off 16.

qa.q: What is VHF channel 70 for, and can I talk on it?
qa.a: **Channel 70** carries only the digital signals of DSC, distress alerts among them. Voice would block them, so the set will not let you talk there; yachts talk on intership channels such as 72 or 77.

blocks.p: **Channel 70** carries only the digital signals of DSC, distress alerts among them: voice there would block them, and the set will not let you talk. **Channel 13** is the bridge-to-bridge channel for the safety of navigation. **Intership** channels such as 72 and 77 are for talk between vessels. Channel 6 is intership too, but it is also used on scene in search and rescue, so leave it free.
Many sets carry an international and a USA channel plan, and some channels differ between them. Outside North America the set must be in international mode: **INT**, not USA, on the display.

qa.q: Why can't I hear the other yacht on a duplex VHF channel?
qa.a: On a **duplex** channel both yachts send on the same frequency and listen on the other, so each hears the coast station but not the other yacht. Ship to ship, use a simplex channel.

blocks.p: On a **simplex** channel everyone sends and listens on one frequency. While you press the button you hear nothing, and if two stations transmit together neither hears the other. So you talk in turn and end each transmission with OVER. Channel 16 and the intership channels are simplex.

parts: pressed: you send, you hear nothing

blocks.p: A **duplex** channel uses two frequencies: a ship sends on one and listens on the other, and the coast station does the opposite. That suits ship-to-shore calls. Two yachts on a duplex channel both send on the same frequency and both listen on the other, so each hears the coast station but not the other yacht.

qa.q: Which VHF channel do I use to call a marina?
qa.a: The marina's own **working channel**, from the pilot book, almanac or chart. Port and marina channels differ from place to place, so look them up before you arrive rather than guess.

blocks.p: If the channel you agreed is busy, do not talk over the others: agree another free intership channel. Port and marina channels differ from place to place, so look them up before you arrive rather than guess. Near a busy commercial port, listen to its port operations or traffic channel as well as 16: you learn what the big ships are about to do.

sections.title: As far as the antenna can see

qa.q: Why can't my friend 6 miles away hear me on VHF?
qa.a: High land in the way stops the signal however close you are. VHF travels roughly in straight lines, so range depends on the **height** of both antennas and a clear path between them.

blocks.p: VHF travels roughly in straight lines, like light. Two things decide whether you are heard: the **height** of both antennas and a **clear path** between them. Yacht to yacht with masthead antennas, count on roughly 10 to 20 miles over open water, not 40.

fig.note: 6 miles apart, but the island blocks the path

blocks.p: High land in the way stops the signal however close you are. A coast station on a mountain is the opposite case: its antenna is so high that it hears you from far off, while friends a few miles away behind a headland do not.

marks: coast station on a mountain, 30 miles north
fig.note: The high station hears you · friends 3 miles away do not

blocks.rule: Height and a clear path give range. Land in between takes it away.
